anti_overlap: fd-wasm-threading-feasibility covers the technical feasibility of in-browser threading
fd-server-side-execution covers the technical design of the WebSocket bridge and server infrastructure costs
fd-hybrid-architecture covers split execution and novel compilation targets
decision_lens: Prioritizes findings that challenge the assumption that sub-50ms ticks are required for the discovery use case, and identifies which performance degradation modes (jank, stutter, slow time-to-first-simulation) are most damaging to discovery user retention versus which are acceptable compromises.
focus: Distribution and discovery UX implications of each execution model: cold start time, install friction, multiplayer/shared-state possibilities, and whether the performance constraints of each approach actually matter for the target discovery use case
name: fd-distribution-ux-tradeoffs
persona: A product engineer who has shipped both native desktop apps and browser-based complex simulations, with experience measuring where users actually drop off during onboarding versus where engineers overestimate performance sensitivity. Evaluates each technical approach through the lens of whether discovery users notice the difference.
review_areas: Whether 50ms-100ms tick latency (realistic for server-hosted or single-threaded WASM) is perceptible to a discovery user watching a geopolitical simulation versus a desktop user who set the tick rate themselves — and what the SimulationStatusLight speed/paused controls reveal about user-controlled time compression

Cold start time analysis for each approach: WASM binary download size for the simulation-engine crate plus its data (baseline manifests, country catalogs), WebSocket connection establishment overhead, and how these compare to a desktop app install

Whether the existing broadcast::channel(64) snapshot channel and watch::channel status model maps cleanly to a browser architecture (SSE, WebSocket, or SharedWorker broadcast) without a full rewrite of the handle/runner boundary

Multiplayer and collaborative play as an emergent capability of the server-hosted approach that the Tauri desktop app cannot offer — whether this is a meaningful differentiator for the discovery use case that justifies server costs

App store vs web distribution friction: whether Tauri's existing tauri-plugin-mcp and desktop packaging actually block discovery relative to a browser URL, and whether a PWA wrapper around the server-hosted approach closes the gap

Fallback and degradation strategy: what a user with a browser that lacks SharedArrayBuffer or WebGPU sees — whether the simulation can detect capabilities and route to server-hosted fallback transparently, using the existing SimulationStatus / SimulationCommand channel design
success_hints: A tick latency threshold above which discovery users would notice degraded simulation speed given the existing speed multiplier system (users can set speed, so absolute tick rate matters less than smoothness at chosen speed)

Identification of whether cold start time or runtime performance is the bigger discovery barrier, which should drive the choice between WASM (slower startup, faster runtime) and server-hosted (faster startup, latency-dependent runtime)
Whether any execution model unlocks a multiplayer or shared-world feature that would be a stronger discovery hook than performance parity with the desktop version
task_context: The simulation has user-controllable speed multipliers and a pause/resume system. The discovery goal is lowering the barrier to trying the simulation. Each execution model trades cold-start time, runtime performance, and infrastructure cost differently.
